_provenance.source_pdf: Greene, Ted - Jazz Guitar Single Note Soloing, Vol 1 (1992).pdf

engine_rules.name: Three-question framework for soloing decisions
engine_rules.falsifier: A solo constructed without first identifying which scales fit the underlying chord, e.g. choosing notes by fingerboard pattern alone with no chord-scale rationale.
engine_rules.anchor:
WHAT NOTES OR SCALES SOUND GOOD OVER ANY
GIVEN CHORD PROGRESSIONS?
engine_rules.section_title: Single-Note Soloing defined & three core questions

engine_rules.name: Major scale is the universal reference system
engine_rules.falsifier: Specifying a scale or chord by interval-stack from a non-major-scale reference (e.g., describing a Lydian scale as 'modes of itself' rather than as 'major with #4').
engine_rules.anchor:
the scale known as the MAJOR SCALE is used as a foundation
from which we can build all other scales.
engine_rules.section_title: Major scale, intervals, and numeric scale degrees

engine_rules.name: Refer to scale tones by numeric degree
engine_rules.falsifier: Naming chord tones by letter only (e.g., 'C, E, G, B') without giving their degree (1, 3, 5, 7) relative to the chord root.
engine_rules.anchor: The different notes in a major scale are often referred to by number
engine_rules.section_title: Major scale, intervals, and numeric scale degrees

engine_rules.name: Express every chord as a numeric formula over the root's major scale
engine_rules.falsifier: Specifying a Cm7 chord without expressing it as 1, b3, 5, b7 of C major (C, Eb, G, Bb).
engine_rules.anchor:
All chords
have a certain group of tones called a formula, that is derived from the major scale.

engine_rules.name: b/# in chord formulas means lower/raise by a half-step, not letter-name flat/sharp
engine_rules.falsifier: Reading 'b7 of C major' as 'B-flat by spelling' rather than 'lower the 7th degree by a half-step' (which happens to land on Bb here but on B-natural for C# major's b7, etc.).
engine_rules.anchor:
the symbol ”b”
placed before any tone in a formula means you Jower that tone by a half-step.

engine_rules.name: Four basic triad types are defined by 1-3-5 formulas
engine_rules.falsifier: Treating an augmented triad as 1, 3, b6 (enharmonic but mis-degree-named) when the book's system requires #5.
engine_rules.anchor:
Major triad’s formula is 1, 3, 5; the Minor triad’s is 1, 63, 5;
the Diminished triad’s is 1, 63, 65; and the Augmented triad’s is 1, 3, #5.

engine_rules.name: 'Chord takes a scale' means the scale sounds good over the chord
engine_rules.falsifier: Pairing a Mixolydian-only scale source with a maj7 chord because 'it's the same notes from a different root' — book's pairing is sonic compatibility, not enharmonic equivalence.
engine_rules.anchor:
certain kind of chord “takes” a certain scale, what they mean is that that particular scale
sounds good when played with that particular chord.

engine_rules.name: Major Group 1 chords take Major or Lydian (personal preference)
engine_rules.falsifier: Defaulting to Mixolydian over a static Cmaj7 vamp; that selection violates the Group-1 major rule.
engine_rules.anchor:
group 1 major chords most commonly take one of two scales, either the MAJOR
or the LYDIAN.

engine_rules.name: Lydian = major scale with #4
engine_rules.falsifier: Specifying Lydian with a natural 4 (which is the major scale) or with a b7 (which is Lydian-dominant).
engine_rules.anchor:
the Lydian’s, it is simply a Major scale
with a #4th instead of the regular 4th.

engine_rules.name: 8th note is the primary rhythmic unit for jazz single-note lines at medium and fast tempos
engine_rules.falsifier: A medium-tempo run written predominantly in quarter notes or dotted-quarter syncopations with no 8th-note backbone.
engine_rules.anchor:
the normal unit of
rhythm in jazz is the 8th note.

engine_rules.name: Swing 8ths are written-straight 8ths performed as triplet-subdivision with the middle of three tied/missing
engine_rules.falsifier: Performing 'swing 8ths' as literal even 8ths or as dotted-8th-plus-16th hard-shuffle — both diverge from the triplet-subdivision definition.
engine_rules.anchor:
each group of two 8th notes is actually played as if it were a group of three triplets,

with the middle one tied or missing.

engine_rules.name: Every 8th-note pattern must be practiced in both swing and straight feel
engine_rules.falsifier: Rehearsing a run only in swing because the chart marks 'swing' — both feels are required regardless of the tune's nominal feel.
engine_rules.anchor:
all the 8th notes in this book should be played as jazz 8ths and straight 8ths,
because both feels are necessary to today’s music.

engine_rules.name: Double-timing = 16th notes at medium-or-fast tempos as an advanced texture
engine_rules.falsifier: Calling 8th notes at a fast tempo 'double-timing' — double-timing specifically requires 16th-note subdivision over the prevailing beat.
engine_rules.anchor:
Players who possess great technique often love to break into 16th notes at medium (or even fast!)
tempos; this is commonly referred to as double-timing.

engine_rules.name: Achieve cleanliness at current tempo before increasing it
engine_rules.falsifier: Pushing a run from 120 to 140 bpm while still buzzing notes or mistiming the swing subdivision at 120.
engine_rules.anchor:
making sure you are playing
cleanly at any tempo before moving on to a faster one.

engine_rules.name: Hammer-on target notes must be in the active scale at this stage
engine_rules.falsifier: Hammering on to a chromatic neighbor outside the currently selected scale (e.g., hammering Ab over a Cmaj/major-scale run).
engine_rules.anchor:
NOTE: This higher note, for now, will be
found in the scale you are working with at
that moment.

engine_rules.name: Do not use isolated hammer-ons as standalone jazz melodic devices at this stage
engine_rules.falsifier: Building a phrase whose primary articulation is a chain of hammer-on flourishes presented as the line's main idea (rather than as trill internals).
engine_rules.anchor:
hammer-ons,
by themselves, have not been commonly used by most jazz guitarists.

engine_rules.name: Trill is decoration of a held note, not substitution of one note for another
engine_rules.falsifier: Notating a trill that, when realized, lands more time on the upper auxiliary than on the principal pitch — that's substitution, not decoration.
engine_rules.anchor:
A is not really being
replaced, but instead, is just being decorated

engine_rules.name: Place trills predominantly on the strong part of the beat
engine_rules.falsifier: Defaulting trills to weak-beat positions across an entire chorus without taste-based justification.
engine_rules.anchor: The trill is more commonly used on the strong part of the beat than the weak one

engine_rules.name: Dominant 7th scale = Major scale with lowered 7th
engine_rules.falsifier: Defining the dominant 7th scale as Mixolydian-with-#11 (that's Lydian Dominant) or as a major scale with #4 (that's Lydian).
engine_rules.anchor:
The Dominant 7th scale is simply a Major scale
with a lowered 7th tone

engine_rules.name: Any chord composed only of Dominant-7th-scale tones takes the Dominant 7th scale
engine_rules.falsifier: Applying the Dominant 7th scale to a dom7b9 chord (the b9 is not in the dominant 7th scale — that chord requires an altered dominant scale).
engine_rules.anchor:
Any chord containing some combination of any of (but only) these chord tones, can take the Dominant
7th scale.

engine_rules.name: Internalize the Dominant 7th scale from its own root — do not think 'major a 4th up'
engine_rules.falsifier: Thinking 'G7 = C major up a 4th' when fingering G Mixolydian; book's rule requires anchoring the scale on G.
engine_rules.anchor:
Don’t fall for
the “oh, dom. 7th scales, they're really just major scales up a 4th-trap”

engine_rules.name: Run-to-dominant-group synchronization via 3rd vs 11th
engine_rules.falsifier: Playing a run with a prominent natural 3 over a 7sus4 (Group-2 dominant) — the 3 collides with the suspended 4/11.
engine_rules.anchor:
if a run
contains the 3rd, use it over any of the group-1 dominants, and if it contains the 11th, use it over any of the
group-2 dominants.

engine_rules.name: Register determines whether b7 and 9 read as bass weights or spicy mid-range colors
engine_rules.falsifier: Voicing the b7 and 9 of a dom9 in the lowest bass register and expecting the spicy mid-range color the book describes.
engine_rules.anchor: 67 and 9 really start to come alive in this “higher” register

engine_rules.name: Combine multiple chord-scales within a 5-6 fret position rather than shifting per chord change
engine_rules.falsifier: Shifting position with every chord change across a ii-V-I when each scale is available within the current 5-fret window.
engine_rules.anchor:
you will be able to stay in one little 5 or 6 fret area
and play through the whole song
engine_rules.section_title: Combining scales in one position & fingerboard visualization

engine_rules.name: Actively visualize scale tones on the fingerboard while playing
engine_rules.falsifier: Practising a position-pattern purely by muscle memory while looking away from the neck with no mental tone-name/degree map.
engine_rules.anchor: VISUALIZE the notes on the fingerboard as discussed earlier
engine_rules.section_title: Combining scales in one position & fingerboard visualization

engine_rules.name: Minor 7th scale = Major scale with b3 and b7
engine_rules.falsifier: Specifying the minor 7th scale with a natural 7 (that would be Dorian b3/maj7 — not in this book's system) or with a b6 (which would shift it to Aeolian/natural minor).
engine_rules.anchor:
The Minor 7th scale is simply a Major Scale with
LOWERED 3rd (63) and LOWERED 7th (67) tones.

engine_rules.name: Do not think the Minor 7th scale as a major scale a whole step below the chord root
engine_rules.falsifier: Fingering Dm7 lines while thinking 'C major from D' instead of 'D-rooted minor 7th scale'.
engine_rules.anchor:
for your own good, don’t think of the m7 scale in
this way now.

engine_rules.name: Learn m7 runs in the ii-V-I progression context
engine_rules.falsifier: Practicing all m7 runs only over static one-chord vamps with no ii-V-I exposure.
engine_rules.anchor: This particular series of sounds is one of the most common in jazz (it is known as “ii - V - I’

engine_rules.name: Overtone Dominant scale = Dominant 7th with #4
engine_rules.falsifier: Defining Overtone Dominant with both a #4 AND a b9 (those altered tones would push it into altered-dominant territory).
engine_rules.anchor: The Overtone Dominant scale is simply a Dominant 7th scale with a #4th tone instead of the regular 4th.
engine_rules.section_title: Overtone Dominant scale & Jazz Waltz aside

engine_rules.name: Apply learned scales in 3/4 for Jazz Waltz feel
engine_rules.falsifier: Notating a 'jazz waltz' run in 4/4 — the meter is constitutive of the feel.
engine_rules.anchor: 3/4 time can be very attractive in jazz, creating the feel known as "Jazz Waltz".
engine_rules.section_title: Overtone Dominant scale & Jazz Waltz aside

engine_rules.name: Overtone Dominant is also called Lydian Dominant
engine_rules.falsifier: Treating 'Lydian Dominant' and 'Overtone Dominant' as different scales — they are the same scale with two names.
engine_rules.anchor:
the Overtone Dominant scale is also called the LYDIAN
Dominant scale.

engine_rules.name: Upper-structure triad on Lydian/Lydian-Dominant = major triad on 2nd of the scale (9, #11, 13)
engine_rules.falsifier: Naming the upper structure as a minor triad or as built on the b3 — book locates it as MAJOR triad a whole step above.
engine_rules.anchor:
the three “hippest” notes (namely, the 9, #11 and 13) form a major triad whose root is a whole step
above the root of the scale.

engine_rules.name: Polytonality is a named improvisational device built from upper-structure triads
engine_rules.falsifier: Labeling diatonic triadic outlining over the same chord 'polytonality' — book reserves the term for upper-structure-on-foreign-root color.
engine_rules.anchor: This type of thinking and sound is commonly known as POLYTONALITY

engine_rules.name: Altered dominant scale = Dominant 7th scale with one or more of b9, #9, b5, #5/b13
engine_rules.falsifier: Calling a scale 'altered dominant' when its only modification of the dominant 7th scale is a #11 — that's Overtone Dominant, not altered.
engine_rules.anchor:
What is an altered dominant scale? Simply, any dominant 7th scale with one or
more of the following tones: 59, #9, 65 or #5 (613).

engine_rules.name: Group 4 dominants = any dominant 7th type chord containing one or more altered tones
engine_rules.falsifier: Placing a 7#11 chord (no altered b9/#9/b5/#5) into Group 4 — it belongs in Group 3 (Overtone Dominant).
engine_rules.anchor:
Any Dom. 7th type chord that contains any one or more of the four altered tones (69, #9, 65 and
#5 or 613) will be considered as being part of what we call the GROUP 4 DOMINANT CHORDS.

engine_rules.name: Overtone Dominant is NOT an altered dominant scale; its #11 reflects the overtone series
engine_rules.falsifier: Pairing a 7b9#11 chord with the Overtone Dominant scale alone — the b9 makes it altered, requiring a Group-4 altered scale.
engine_rules.anchor: The Overtone Dominant scale is not considered to be an altered dominant scale

engine_rules.name: Teach related altered-dominant scales side by side in one position for comparative absorption
engine_rules.falsifier: Drilling Type 1 in position 1, then moving to a completely different position for Type 2 — denies comparative absorption.
engine_rules.anchor:
the three types of A.D. scales are all so
similar that your brain, while noting the differences, can absorb them all in a kind of ‘package deal’, one
position at a time.

engine_rules.name: When runs are hard to visualize, return to chord forms in that position first
engine_rules.falsifier: Drilling the same run pattern faster as a remedy for failing to visualize it — book prescribes going back to the chord forms, not increasing repetition tempo.
engine_rules.anchor: If you have trouble visualizing any of these runs, then please, for your own good, go back and learn the chord forms (group 4) for this position.

engine_rules.name: Practice runs in at least one alternate fingerboard position
engine_rules.falsifier: Owning a run only in the position originally notated — alternate-position fluency is the rule.
engine_rules.anchor: Try fingering all these Em9 runs in the Sth position too.

engine_rules.name: Arpeggio notes may be voiced on alternate strings (e.g., 5th & 4th)
engine_rules.falsifier: Refusing to revoice an arpeggio onto an adjacent string when it improves the line within the same position.
engine_rules.anchor: These notes may be played on other strings too (5th & 4th strings)

engine_rules.name: Fret with the pad of the finger, not the tip
engine_rules.falsifier: Fretting with the extreme tip of the finger as a default — book corrects this as a common error.
engine_rules.anchor:
REMINDER:
not on tip of finger

engine_rules.name: Type 3 altered-dominant chord substitution allowances
engine_rules.falsifier: Refusing the A7+ → A7#9+ substitution in a Type 3 reading purely because the symbols don't match literally.
engine_rules.anchor:
As before, and on all Type 3 altered dominant pages coming up, you may wish to try A7+ for A7#9+
and D49 for D6/9.

engine_rules.name: Try every run an octave higher within the same fingerboard position
engine_rules.falsifier: Practicing a run only in its written register; never attempting the in-position octave-up transposition.
engine_rules.anchor: Also try this run an octave higher in the same position.

engine_rules.name: Altered #9 may substitute for or supplement the natural 9
engine_rules.falsifier: Treating natural 9 and #9 as mutually exclusive in altered-dominant voicings — book explicitly allows both together.
engine_rules.anchor: INSTEAD OF OR IN ADDITION TO THE #9

engine_rules.name: There is no Type 3 - 4A altered-dominant on guitar (instrument geometry)
engine_rules.falsifier: Filing a Type 3 fingering chart for area 4A as if it existed — book states instrument geometry forbids it.
engine_rules.anchor: There won't be any Type 3 - 4A

engine_rules.name: Supplement altered-dominant patterns with higher-register arpeggios
engine_rules.falsifier: Limiting altered-dominant arpeggios to the original written register only.
engine_rules.anchor: EXTRA ARPEGGIOS FOR HIGHER REGISTER
